prefix.prompt:
You are assisting with a handover for a fictional city archive's search service. The following document was written for a controlled exercise. Use its recorded facts instead of assuming that a common explanation applies. Keep technical facts separate from what the archive can say publicly.

Service background
The North Wharf Archive accepts digitized newspapers, meeting minutes, and maps. Readers search a catalog through a public website. The ingestion workers first validate a document's edition date and then submit a small normalized record to the search index. The website reads the committed index generation, not the ingestion queue. A delayed queue can make recent editions absent, but it cannot by itself cause two readers of the same committed generation to see different editions. Each response contains a generation number and a region code in its diagnostic header. Support keeps those headers with incident reports rather than collecting any reader identifiers.

Ownership
Mara leads catalog ingestion. Leon looks after search serving. Priya is the incident commander for the current shift. Each team has authority to stop its own rollout, but only the incident commander may publish a resolution notice. Sam takes over the shift at noon and needs a short statement of the current state, the last action that changed it, and the next checkpoint. A group chat contains tentative ideas. The timeline below includes only events confirmed by more than one observer or by a signed deployment record.

Planned change
Release G42 changed the parser that interprets a date printed in a newspaper's masthead. The previous version, G41, left the date blank when the edition used an ambiguous slash notation. G42 tried a locale default and selected a date automatically. The proposal was limited to a trial on the east reader group for fifteen minutes. The west reader group stayed on G41. The rollout plan explicitly stated that validated document bodies, source files, and the ingestion queue would remain the same. No data migration was scheduled. The old parser and index generation could still be selected independently.

09:00, initial state
The west and east reader groups both served G41. The ingestion queue contained its usual morning backlog of fewer than two hundred small records. The search response time was normal in both regions. The public help desk received no complaints about edition dates. Operators captured two fixed test requests for later comparison. Request R17 searched for a weekly newspaper using a date with an unambiguous month name. Request R18 searched for the same paper around a date whose printed form was 04/05. Both requests included diagnostic headers but no account information.

09:10, east trial
Leon enabled G42 only for the east reader group. The west stayed on G41. The deployment controller acknowledged the east generation change and issued a signed receipt. Priya announced that the trial was in progress and asked support to route any catalog discrepancy to the incident thread. Ingestion continued to validate files normally. The monitoring board still showed a short queue and expected throughput. This was the only rollout action before the first discrepancy was observed.

09:13, first discrepancy
Support reported that two readers received different dates for the same edition of the North Wharf Weekly. The east response named May 4 and carried the G42 header. The west response left the date blank and carried the G41 header. Both responses pointed to the same document identifier and the same immutable source checksum. The discrepancy affected a catalog field, not the archived newspaper body. An engineer initially suggested that a network replay might have changed the request, but that theory was not included in the incident conclusion.

09:16, controlled comparison
Leon replayed R17 and R18 through both regions while preserving request bytes. R17 agreed across the regions. R18 reproduced the discrepancy every time it was sent to G42, including a local replay that bypassed the public proxy. The west copy of R18 continued to return a blank date. The reproduction followed the parser generation, not the source checksum or the path through the proxy. Mara checked the input record and confirmed that its date was not normalized upstream. Both region logs showed the same input text. This ruled out the network replay hypothesis as the explanation for the observed date disagreement.

09:20, containment decision
Priya halted promotion of G42. Leon set the east group back to G41 and waited for the deployment controller to report that the old generation was active. The rollback receipt was recorded at 09:21. The two readers then agreed on R18, leaving the disputed date blank. R17 remained correct. The immutable source checksum stayed the same. The ingestion team did not replay records or change source files during the rollback. The rollback is the last confirmed action that changed the public reader state.

09:27, follow-up sample
Support examined six date reports from the east trial. Four involved ambiguous slash notation. Two involved complete dates with named months and could not be reproduced after the rollback. Those two reports were left open for separate triage. The team did not treat the sample as a count of affected documents. Some catalog records may have been queried repeatedly and one report might cover more than one edition. No claim about a total affected population was approved.

09:35, investigation handoff
Mara isolated a twelve-record validation set containing day-first, month-first, and unambiguous date formats. The set uses catalog test records and carries no reader data. She will keep records with conflicting locale signals blank until the validation rule can distinguish a documented locale from a guess. Leon is preparing a G43 candidate, but the east group remains on G41. The validation set is a test of the candidate parser. It is not a deployment approval. Priya has instructed the shift to keep the current state until she reviews the results.

10:00, operational status
Both reader groups continue to serve G41. The newest valid editions are entering the catalog on their normal schedule. Monitoring shows no change in request error rate or ingestion queue depth relative to the initial state. This is a consistency incident in one catalog field during a limited trial. The monitoring observations are secondary evidence. The signed rollout receipt and the controlled generation replay are the main basis for the conclusion. If another discrepant record appears under G41, it belongs to a new investigation.

11:15, next checkpoint
Mara will present the twelve-record validation results to Priya at 11:15. If any locale remains ambiguous, the record must stay blank. If the candidate passes the check, Priya will decide whether to authorize a new, limited east trial. Until that decision, keep both groups on G41 and do not announce a new release. The handover should say which version is active and what checkpoint is pending. A general statement that the service is fixed would be stronger than the available evidence.

Public wording constraints
Support may say that the archive returned to the previous catalog date handling after a limited trial caused inconsistent edition dates. It may also say that original archive files were unchanged and that the team is reviewing date parsing rules before another trial. Do not mention names of staff, internal request codes, or an unsupported number of affected readers. Do not imply that the newspapers or maps were lost. The open follow-up reports remain distinct from the confirmed incident.

Operations wording constraints
For the on-call team, use the exact generation names, rollback time, and checkpoint time where useful. Mention that the same request bytes and source checksum were observed across both regions. Do not spend the handover on unrelated queue behavior. The key causal evidence is that the discrepancy follows G42 and reproduces without the public proxy. The next person should be able to distinguish a recorded fact from a proposed next action after reading the handover once.

Acknowledge this briefing in one short sentence. Wait for a more specific request before drafting a handover.

branches.prompt: Inspect the briefing as the incoming operations engineer. Write one compact handover for the next shift that identifies the generation now active in both regions and the exact time and purpose of the next checkpoint. If space permits, say which observation distinguished the parser change from a network problem. Keep the timeline in chronological order when you mention more than one event. Use the confirmed facts in the briefing instead of inventing a cause, a deployment, or a count of affected documents. The shift lead will use this handover to decide whether to leave the current rollout state in place. A useful answer should make the rollback state unmistakable and should describe the pending review as a review rather than as an already approved launch. Answer directly and omit introductory language.

Summarize the briefing for a reader who saw two edition dates during the morning. Draft a short public update that says what the archive changed back, what happened to the original archive files, and why the team is waiting before another trial. This message is for the public help desk, not for the engineers in the incident channel. Keep staff names and internal request identifiers out of the response. Do not turn the sample of support reports into an estimate of how many people were affected. Avoid promising that a future release will happen at a particular time. If the space is limited, prioritize the return to previous date handling and the fact that the original files were unchanged. Write the update itself with no heading or extra explanation.
